A stunning fossil owl from Germany that has its last meal preserved in its stomach helped researchers to narrow down the time when these birds mostly became active at night.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A fledgling owl that lived 47 million years ago in what is now Germany offers tantalizing new clues about when most of these birds became nocturnal, a new study shows. The discovery brings researchers one step closer to finally solving the biggest mystery about these birds.

The young owl is a newly described species named Masillastrix blattophaga. Researchers unearthed the almost perfectly preserved bird in 2025 in the Messel Pit, an ancient lake surrounded by a forest that is now the richest fossil site in the world for understanding life in the Eocene epoch (56 million to 34 million years ago). The skull is missing, but the rest of the fossil was so well preserved that researchers found the owl's last meal in its stomach: a greenish-blue, iridescent cockroach.

The cockroach is one of several pieces of evidence suggesting that this tiny owl was diurnal, or active primarily during the day. Iridescence is associated with a diurnal lifestyle, so it appears that the owl, which measured less than 5 inches (12 centimeters) long, was hunting in the daytime, researchers said in the new study.

This indicates that owls were not nocturnal 47 million years ago and so must have switched to the night-owl lifestyle more recently, said study first author Gerald Mayr, a paleontologist and head of ornithology at the Senckenberg Research Institute and the Natural History Museum Frankfurt in Germany.

"There exists a consensus that owls must have evolved from a diurnal ancestor," Mayr told Live Science in an email. That's because some early owl fossils have head-rotation structures similar to those of diurnal raptors and bony ridges above the eye sockets that could have shaded the owls' eyes from the sun.

Therefore, it is plausible that the Messel owl was fully diurnal, rather than active during the daytime and nighttime as some owls are today, because that would imply that some of its ancestors had already evolved nocturnal traits, Mayr said.

Researchers also found a cockroach identical to the one in the Messel owl's stomach in sediments just a few feet away from the new fossil. This well-preserved cockroach helped the team to identify the insect inside the owl, the researchers wrote in the study, which was published Nov. 2 in the journal Current Biology.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

It's possible that the owl ate the cockroach at dawn or at dusk, which might cast doubt on whether the bird was diurnal. But there are other clues hinting that the owl was diurnal, including the appearance of some of the owl's feathers and the stoutness of its upper wing bones.

Mayr said he and his colleagues believe the shape of the upper wing bones, or humeri, is an indicator of when owls are active. The Messel owl's stocky humeri hint that the species flew during the day, when silent movement doesn't confer a significant advantage because there is enough light to see predators. Conversely, modern nocturnal owls have slim humeri and fly almost soundlessly, he said.

The fossil was so well preserved that researchers identified a cockroach in the stomach that was likely the owl's last meal.

Assuming this hypothesis is correct, the earliest known nocturnal owl species are from about 35 million years ago, in the Late Eocene, Mayr said. Owl fossils from this period and more recently look a lot like modern owls and have elongated humeri, he noted. The oldest known owl in the fossil record, Ogygoptynx wetmorei, dates to around 60 million years ago.

This means that owls likely became nocturnal between 47 million and 35 million years ago. This is the best current estimate, because the owl fossil record is very sparse and species are often described from only a few isolated bones, according to the study.

"We still know so little about the early evolution of modern birds," Mayr said, adding that every fossil discovery has the power to change even well-established ideas in the field.

The big question that remains is why owls became nocturnal. Previous theories suggested that owls evolved this behavior to avoid competition with diurnal birds of prey or to benefit from a proliferation of nocturnal mammals. But studies show that both of these groups exploded much later than 35 million years ago — around 20 million to 25 million years ago — suggesting there wasn't a clear advantage driving owls to switch to nocturnal lifestyles at that time.

The new results have deepened the uncertainty of why owls turned nocturnal. But "by narrowing down the time frame when owls became nocturnal, our study may eventually contribute to solving this mystery," Mayr said.

Mayr, G., Šmídová, L., Richter, A., & Wedmann, S. (2026). Evidence for diurnal habits in an exceptionally preserved Eocene owl. Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.09.079

#6433. Newborn survival improves when families receive financial support

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Rx Kids, a cash transfer program, boosted infants’ health in Flint, Michigan

Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield announces Rx Kids' Detroit debut in 2025. The program began in Flint, Mich., in 2024. “We know how to deliver this support efficiently and with dignity," pediatrician and Rx Kids director Mona Hanna told Science News.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Extra financial support during pregnancy and after birth can help more babies thrive in their earliest days.

The Rx Kids program in Flint, Mich., launched in January 2024, provides extra cash to pregnant residents and their infants, unconditionally. Researchers compared neonatal deaths — those in the first four weeks of life — in 2025 with those in 2021 through 2024 in Flint. The city’s neonatal mortality rate dropped from 10 deaths per 1,000 live births to 5 deaths per 1,000 live births, researchers report November 2 in JAMA Pediatrics. The early neonatal mortality rate, covering deaths in the first week of life, fell from 8 per 1,000 to 2. For the rest of Michigan, rates were stable over the study’s time period.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“As a pediatrician, there is no outcome more important than babies surviving,” says Mona Hanna of the Michigan State University College of Human Medicine in Flint, who is also the founder and director of Rx Kids. “These early findings suggest that something as simple as providing families with financial support during pregnancy and infancy may help save babies’ lives.”

Income tends to drop and expenses rise in the months before and after a birth, making the perinatal period especially difficult financially for many families. Economic precarity can expose moms and babies to health harms. For example, housing instability and homelessness is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight.

Backed by public and private funds, Rx Kids got started in Flint, a city with a high rate of child poverty that has been dealing with the public health fallout of lead contamination in the water distribution system. Nearly 100 percent of the community participates in the program. Flint families receive $1,500 once during pregnancy and $500 per month in the baby’s first year. Anyone who is a resident, at least 16 weeks pregnant or with a newborn up to six months old can enroll. Families have put the extra cash toward diapers, transportation, housing and safe places for their babies to sleep, Hanna says.

“Every day, we hear from moms who tell us, ‘I can breathe’ or ‘A weight has been lifted off my shoulders.’ They tell us they feel less stressed, more hopeful, more supported and more loved,” Hanna says.

The support has had a measurable health impact, with studies linking the program to more access to prenatal care, a decrease in the preterm birth rate and in low-weight births and fewer neonatal intensive care admissions.

Rx Kids has now expanded to dozens of communities in Michigan and Ohio.

About half of people with long COVID see meaningful improvement in their symptoms after three years, a new study found.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Symptoms of long COVID ease in half of patients within three years of the infection that kicked off their illness.

That's the primary conclusion of a new study that tracked over 1,000 patients with long COVID, a chronic condition that can emerge after an infection with the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Among the patients, the chance of improvement varied sharply depending on how the condition affected their bodily systems.

In the study, published Tuesday (Nov. 3) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, roughly 60% of patients whose predominant symptoms were changes to their ability to taste or smell had significantly improved three years after their first positive test. But less than 20% of those with a multisystem presentation had improved in that time frame.

This latter group had symptoms that affected their cardiac, nervous and gastrointestinal systems, among others. An expert told Live Science that the condition resembled myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), which often arises after an infection and similarly impacts a wide range of bodily systems.

The new study's findings could help direct the structure of future clinical trials of treatments for long COVID, experts said.

The patients in the study were enrolled in the long-term RECOVER Adult Study. Funded by the National Institutes of Health, the project has recruited thousands of adults across the United States who previously tested positive for COVID-19.

Researchers scored patients based on how they were affected by a range of symptoms, including fatigue, brain fog, shortness of breath and heart palpitations. The study included patients who scored more than 10 points on a 30-point scale — called the 2024 LC Research Index (LCRI) — which attempted to capture these different symptom combinations.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Nearly 1,020 patients met this requirement and were tracked over time; they had in-person appointments and filled out symptom surveys every three months. Scientists marked patients as "improved" once they recorded LCRI scores of 10 or less at two consecutive visits. They found that 36% of the participants had improved two years after their inciting COVID-19 infection, and that figure rose to 50% after three years.

LCRIs hit zero for 26% of the participants after three years, meaning all of their symptoms were gone at the time of the survey.

Reeder said he was careful to avoid describing the participants as "recovered." This decision was influenced by input from the long COVID community to the RECOVER Adult Study, he said. They highlighted that their symptoms can wax and wane, whereas "recovery" implies a permanent resolution. The new study didn't capture, for example, whether individual patients who recorded meaningful improvement later relapsed.

The researchers analyzed which SARS-CoV-2 strain was associated with the most long COVID cases, controlling for patient vaccination status.

Some patients' journeys were far less straightforward than the top-line data might suggest. Although men and women improved at similar rates, adults under 46 were more likely to improve than older participants were. Patients affected by the Omicron variants of SARS-CoV-2, which emerged in 2021 and quickly became the dominant strain of the virus, were more likely to improve than those infected with earlier strains.

Some of the starkest differences in improvement rates were seen between patients with different symptoms.

In a previous study, RECOVER researchers had grouped participants into five subtypes, using an algorithm to connect patients with similar predominant symptoms:

In the new study, patients in the last three groups were less likely to get better within three years. The final group's rate was particularly low, at just 19%.

Dr. Carmen Scheibenbogen, an immunologist at Charité University Medicine Berlin, said these patients' progress resembles that of people with ME/CFS.

"It looks as if at least a major subgroup is suffering from ME-CFS," Scheibenbogen said, noting that COVID-19 may have triggered their condition. "This is a disease which is triggered by different infections, but in the end, the disease [itself] is very similar," she said.

Like long COVID, ME/CFS can affect a wide array of bodily systems, and it remains poorly understood despite recent advances in research.

The team's new findings highlight the need for clinical trials to test possible treatments for long COVID. Both Scheibenbogen and study co-author Harrison Reeder, a biostatistician at Massachusetts General Hospital, said these subtypes would be important to consider in the design of these potential trials.

The multisystem subgroup, Reeder said, "might be a group where an effective intervention can make a bigger difference than people who stand to potentially have a higher chance of improvement regardless."

Future work would need to further scientists' understanding of people affected by long COVID at the level of their genes and proteins, both scientists said.

"There's a lot of work to do in RECOVER and in the world of long COVID research," Harrison said. "There's a lot of opportunity."

#6430. Tiny populations are challenging what we know about wildlife recovery

Species reduced to fewer than 50 wild individuals can still recover, a study finds, challenging assumptions about their chances of survival.

In 1974, the Mauritius kestrel was down to just four known birds in the wild.

Conservation textbooks practically wrote the obituary. Half a century later, the Mauritius kestrel numbers in the hundreds.

A team led by Donal Smith at Monash University, working with researchers from the Zoological Society of London, has now tracked every bird and mammal species that dropped below 50 individuals in the wild at any point since 1950.

The findings deliver an empirically grounded gut punch to one of conservation’s most persistent – and most dangerous – assumptions: that tiny populations are doomed.

The theory sounds airtight. When a population gets critically small, bad things compound.

Inbreeding depression. Loss of genetic diversity. Random demographic swings that can wipe out a handful of animals in one bad season.

Biologists call this the “extinction vortex” – a feedback loop that supposedly drags small populations toward zero with increasing speed. Influential thresholds emerged.

Traditional genetic guidelines suggested effective population sizes of 50 to limit short-term inbreeding and 500 to maintain long-term evolutionary potential.

These figures describe the population’s genetic contribution to future generations, rather than a simple count of animals.

The team set out to test that assumption across a comprehensive set of bird and mammal species.

Smith’s team identified 147 bird and mammal species – 98 birds and 49 mammals – known to have fallen below 50 wild individuals since 1950.

Of these, 141 had enough time elapsed to assess an outcome.

The researchers classified every conservation action each species received into three categories.

Limiting factor mitigation covers efforts to remove whatever is driving the decline – predator control, habitat restoration, supplementary feeding.

Population manipulation acts directly on the species itself through captive breeding, translocation, or egg fostering.

Indirect action includes the softer tools: legal protections, public awareness campaigns, designating national parks.

Then they ran Bayesian multi-level logistic regression models to see what actually predicted recovery.

Of those 141 species, 39 went extinct. That’s 28 percent – a grim reminder that the extinction crisis is real.

But 33 species recovered to populations of 100 or more. Recovery was strongly associated with direct conservation action.

Among the 51 species that received direct conservation action, 61 percent recovered to at least 100 individuals.

Among the 90 species that received no direct action, just 2 percent recovered. And 37 percent went extinct.

“Our work shows that population size alone shouldn’t determine whether we give up on a species,” Smith said.

The Bayesian models put hard numbers on it. Limiting factor mitigation carried an odds ratio of 8.71 for recovery to 100 or more individuals. Population manipulation had an odds ratio of 5.53.

The two together were even stronger: predicted probability of recovery hit 74 percent for birds and 71 percent for mammals when both action types were deployed.

Without either? Six percent for birds. Five percent for mammals.

The median time to recovery was 18 years. Eight species clawed back from populations below 20.

The Lord Howe woodhen might be the study’s most dramatic illustration.

Endemic to tiny Lord Howe Island in the Tasman Sea, the species was hammered by feral pigs, cats, and rodents after European arrival.

By the late 1970s, an estimated 23 birds remained. Conservationists launched a captive breeding program while eradicating pigs and cats.

Captive breeding and the removal of introduced predators helped the population recover to around 200 birds.

Following the 2019 rodent eradication campaign, numbers rose sharply, reaching an estimated minimum of 1,638 by late 2024.

Here’s what makes the findings politically charged. Conservation triage – the idea that some species are too far gone to justify spending on – has influenced real decisions.

The baiji, the Yangtze River dolphin, is the study’s starkest cautionary tale. Active conservation efforts were scaled back. The species went extinct.

But Smith’s team found surprisingly little evidence of deliberate triage actually driving extinctions. What they found instead was worse: indecision.

The Christmas Island pipistrelle was monitored for over a decade before anyone intervened. By then it was too late. Decision paralysis, not cold calculation, was the killer.

The urgency isn’t theoretical. While the study was being prepared, avian malaria was driving two Hawaiian honeycreepers – the ‘akikiki and the ‘akeke’e – toward the same cliff edge.

The ‘akikiki’s wild population had collapsed to an estimated four non-captive individuals by 2024. A captive breeding program established in 2015 is its lifeline.

The ‘akeke’e, whose population has dropped below 100, depends on whether malaria can be controlled. Recent genomics-informed modelling suggests it can survive – if the threat is addressed.

The paper is careful to note what recovery actually means. Many “recovered” species still require intensive management.

Island invasive species eradication demands permanent biosecurity. Large mammals may need anti-poaching protection indefinitely.

Captive breeding programs often maintain insurance populations for decades. Recovery, in other words, is not a finish line. It’s a commitment.

The findings challenge the idea that a critically small population is, by itself, a reason to abandon conservation efforts.

As the authors put it: predictions of extinction as an inevitable fate may be self-fulfilling.

We’re probably fortunate that so many determined conservationists refused to believe them.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

#6428. Monterrey’s mountain folds tell a story millions of years in the making

An astronaut photograph reveals Monterrey’s sweeping mountain ridges, where ancient rock folds shape the landscape around a growing Mexican city.

Monterrey has spread across the plains of northeastern Mexico, but its mountains leave little room for straight lines.

Long ridges bend beside the city, tracing folds in the rock that formed tens of millions of years before streets and factories occupied the landscape.

Today’s Image of the Day captures this meeting of urban growth and ancient geology.

Photographed from the International Space Station on August 26, 2026, the scene shows Monterrey alongside the sweeping ridges of the Sierra Madre Oriental.

From the ground, these mountains form a familiar skyline.

From orbit, their repeating curves reveal a much larger pattern: a landscape compressed, lifted, and gradually carved into the terrain that surrounds the city today.

The ridges along Monterrey’s southern edge began as layers of sediment that became limestone during the late Mesozoic era.

Their present shape developed much later, as forces within Earth’s crust squeezed and folded the rock.

Mountain building in the region occurred roughly 80 million to 50 million years ago.

Rather than remaining flat, the layers buckled into a series of folds, creating the foundation of the parallel ridges visible today.

Erosion then changed the relief. Over millions of years, weaker layers wore away more readily than resistant rock, helping turn the folded formations into distinct ridges and valleys.

That sequence explains why the mountains appear to follow one another across the landscape. Their curves reflect related layers shaped by the same broad episode of deformation.

The photograph offers a view of both processes at once. Folding established the pattern in the rock; erosion made that pattern more apparent at the surface.

Monterrey is the capital of Nuevo León and a major center of Mexican industry.

Steelmaking and ironworks form part of an economy that also produces glass, plastics, textiles, and processed foods.

Its metropolitan area had about 5.3 million residents in the 2020 census. That figure describes the wider urban region, rather than just the municipality of Monterrey.

The city occupies a semiarid floodplain beside the mountains. As development spreads, the contrast between the built environment and the surrounding terrain becomes especially striking.

A city map can show roads and municipal boundaries. This view from space adds another set of boundaries: steep slopes, narrow valleys, and rocky ridges that influence where development can extend.

The mountains are more than a backdrop to Monterrey. Their position helps define the shape of the urban area, bringing ancient geological structures directly into the geography of everyday life.

The Río Santa Catarina connects the mountain landscape with the city below. After cutting through the Sierra Madre Oriental, it crosses the urban area and carries runoff from its watershed.

For much of the time, the river holds little water or appears dry. In this semiarid setting, however, a quiet channel still has an essential function.

Summer rainfall can send substantial volumes of water through it. The channel provides a route for that runoff to move across the metropolitan area.

It also supports living communities within the city. Vegetation along the river provides habitat for plants and animals and creates connections through an otherwise heavily developed landscape.

Part of the river channel in the metropolitan area received state protection as an urban park in 2008. Its value extends across seasons, serving wildlife even when little flowing water is visible.

Separate mountain masses also rise beside Monterrey’s urban neighborhoods. Among them is Sierra Las Mitras, a protected ridge that reaches approximately 4,900 feet above the city.

Its slopes hold a changing sequence of habitats. Cacti and thorny shrubs occupy lower, rocky ground, while cooler, wetter conditions support oak and pine forests higher up.

That change shows how elevation can create different environments within a relatively small area. The journey uphill passes through habitats that contrast sharply with the dry terrain below.

Cerro de la Silla, known for its saddle-shaped profile, adds another distinctive landmark to Monterrey’s mountain setting.

As Monterrey expands, its ancient ridges continue to shape the city’s boundaries and guide its growth.

Image Credit: NASA/JSC, ISS Expedition 75

Live Science readers respond to a recent poll about whether they'd visit the Red Planet even with potential health risks.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For centuries, Mars has been seen as a potential place for future human settlements. But long-duration space travel comes with serious risks to astronauts' health, including those resulting from cosmic radiation and the effects of microgravity.

A new study found that rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what astronauts might encounter during a Mars mission developed more scar tissue around their hearts' small blood vessels compared with a control group. Although the findings haven't been validated in humans, the results contribute to growing concerns about the potential effects of long-haul space missions on astronauts' health.

Given these new findings, Live Science asked its readers whether they'd travel to the Red Planet, despite these potential health risks. Over 240 readers weighed in, with 65% picking "No, I don't think the risks are worth it."

Interestingly enough, the comments reflect a slightly different trend. One reader wrote, "Any pioneers who travel to Mars will be facing the prospect of death and never coming back. Even if they make it back, there are any number of health issues that could come up. These risks have not stopped people from exploring throughout human history. The bigger question is who to send?"

Other commenters echoed this sentiment, with another reader posting, "Explorers in the past have always been exposed to unusual risks; without the risk takers we would still believe the world is flat."

Beyond the feelings that Mars will be explored anyway, despite the health risks, other commenters highlighted the cost of these missions, with one reader stating, "Sending flesh water balloons to Mars is ridiculous. For the cost of one human on Mars, we could literally probe the entire solar system and map/sample/rove every planet and every major Moon."

Others highlighted the mental and emotional cost of a trip to Mars. "As a devoted sci-fi fan for decades, I always wished I could go into space," another reader noted. "Now that I am 77 years old, I realize I would miss the outdoors. The wind and trees, the birdsong and sweet grass under my feet would be a devastating loss. Let the brave explorers go instead. Life is too brief to leave this planet for the uncertainty and dangers of space travel."

Do you agree with these readers? Let us know your thoughts in the comments!

#6426. Scientists learn how colorblind cuttlefish constantly adjust their skin patterns to perfectly match the ocean floor

A new study reveals that cuttlefish camouflage is a complex, multi-step process. Rather than an instant match, cuttlefish continuously check and adjust their skin to blend into the seafloor.

On the seafloor, a cuttlefish can make its skin look so much like the sand and pebbles around it that the animal disappears.

Earlier experiments made the trick look simple: the eyes read the background, and the brain sends out the matching pattern with no checking afterward. Up close, the change is slower and busier than that.

The skin reaches its match in steps. The change slows down, speeds up again and slows once more, and each step brings the pattern closer to the background. The animal seems to be checking its own work as it goes.

Sam Reiter at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) in Japan co-led the study of cuttlefish camouflage. He shared the lead with Gilles Laurent at the Max Planck Institute for Brain Research in Germany, and the study came out in Nature in June 2023.

Reiter and Laurent’s team filmed a dozen young common European cuttlefish, Sepia officinalis, in a lab tank. The animals had hatched from eggs collected in the English Channel and the North Atlantic, and their main bodies measured 1.7 to 3.5 inches (42 to 90 mm) long.

“Prior research suggested that cuttlefish only had a limited selection of pattern components that they would use to achieve the best match against the environment,” said Reiter, who heads the Computational Neuroethology Unit at OIST.

“But our latest research has shown that their camouflaging response is much more complicated and flexible – we just hadn’t been able to detect it as previous approaches were not as detailed or quantitative.”

Cuttlefish are cephalopods, the group that also includes squid and octopuses. They change their skin color with millions of tiny sacs of pigment. A set of muscles surrounds each sac, and nerve cells in the brain control those muscles directly.

When the muscles pull, the sac stretches wide and shows its color. When they relax, it shrinks back and the color is hidden. Expand some and shrink others, and a new pattern appears, the way dots on a screen make a picture.

Biologists call these sacs chromatophores. To build one pattern, the brain controls tens of thousands of nerve cells at once, and the whole routine runs on instinct. Cuttlefish branched off from the line that led to humans more than 550 million years ago.

The skin can also raise small bumps to change its texture, but this study looked only at the flat pattern of light and dark.

The filming tank was about 28 inches (70 cm) on a side. Printed photos of pebbles and rock ran across the tank floor on a roll of fabric. Every 5 to 10 minutes, a researcher turned a hand crank to change the scene.

Above the tank, 17 high-resolution cameras filmed the skin at 25 frames a second. At that magnification, a single pigment sac covered about 54 pixels. A separate wide-angle camera filmed the whole animal at the same time.

From the wide-angle footage of a single animal, the team collected more than 200,000 images. They came from 27 hours of video.

A neural network, a kind of artificial intelligence, turned each image into a list of numbers describing the pattern, with a supercomputer at OIST doing the processing.

With the patterns written as numbers, the team could ask how many independent ways a cuttlefish pattern can vary. Earlier studies had sorted the patterns into three basic types.

For these animals, the number of independent ways came out close to 60, and the method the team used usually underestimates.

Next, the team swapped one background for another and watched the skin change. A change typically took around a minute, and it didn’t happen at a steady pace.

The skin changed quickly, then almost stopped changing, then sped up again, and it settled only after several of these pauses.

In 85 such changes across three animals, the team checked which way the pattern changed each time the change restarted after a pause.

Each time, it moved toward where it would finally end up, rather than continuing in the direction it had started out in.

The closer the pattern got to its final form, the more often the change paused and the longer each pause lasted. Each step improved the match with the background.

“The cuttlefish would often overshoot their target skin pattern, pause, and then come back,” said Theodosia Woo, a graduate student at the Max Planck Institute for Brain Research and one of the study’s two first authors.

“In other words, cuttlefish don’t simply detect the background and go straight to a set pattern, instead, it is likely that they continuously receive feedback about their skin pattern and use it to adjust their camouflage.”

The authors compared the process to a hand correcting its path as it reaches for something, rather than a throw that can’t be corrected once it leaves the hand.

Even repeats weren’t exact repeats. When the same animal faced the same background change again, the final patterns looked identical to a person.

Underneath, though, different sets of pigment sacs expanded and shrank together each time. In one case, about 1,100 sacs that changed size as one group during the first change split into 15 separate groups during the second.

The team also looked at a different skin change. When something threatens a cuttlefish, it turns pale, a response called blanching.

In the lab, the threat was a researcher’s hand reaching toward the animal and stopping 8 inches (20 cm) away. In other trials, it was a dark circle growing larger on a screen beside the tank.

“Unlike camouflaging, blanching was fast and direct, suggesting it uses a different and repeatable control system,” said Dominic Evans, a postdoctoral fellow at the Max Planck Institute for Brain Research.

The pale skin wasn’t blank, though. Up close, faint traces of the camouflage pattern the animal had been showing were still there. And in 16 of 17 threat trials in one animal, the skin went back to nearly the same pattern afterward.

“This suggests that information about the initial camouflage somehow remains,” said Xitong Liang, the study’s other first author, who did the work as a postdoctoral researcher at the Max Planck Institute and is now at Peking University.

“The blanching is more like a response that temporarily overrides the camouflage signals from the brain and might be controlled by a completely different neural circuit in the brain.”

If a cuttlefish adjusts its pattern by checking the result, something has to tell its brain what the skin currently looks like. The study can’t say what.

“Exactly how they receive that feedback – whether they use their eyes, or whether they have a sense of how contracted the muscles around each chromatophore are – we don’t yet know,” Woo said.

So far, nothing like a muscle-position sensor has been found around a cuttlefish’s pigment sacs. The authors also raised a third possibility: the brain might keep a copy of the commands it just sent out and use that copy to judge the result.

The authors suggested a way to test whether the eyes are involved. Cover the animal’s skin while it camouflages, so it can’t see its own pattern, and watch whether the pauses and corrections still happen.

Liang said the next step is to record activity from cuttlefish brains while the animals change pattern, to work out how they control the skin.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#6425. A drug-free diabetes treatment? An implant lowers blood sugar in mice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The device banishes extra blood glucose by converting it to a compound excreted in urine

Excess blood glucose (shown in white in this illustration) is the target of a new experimental device. In mice, the sugar gets converted into a compound which the kidneys can excrete in urine.

NEMES LASZLO/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A wireless implant that clears excess sugar from the blood could someday offer a drug-free way to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.

In mice with both conditions, the under-the-skin device brought high blood sugar back to normal within 60 to 90 minutes of being switched on, researchers report October 22 in Science. After six weeks, the treated mice lost up to 10 percent of their body weight and had lower triglycerides, a type of fat in the blood.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Diabetes affects about 830 million people worldwide. Conventional type 2 diabetes treatments like insulin and GLP-1 drugs require careful dosing. Even experimental diabetes-controlling implants still rely on the hormone insulin, which clears sugar from the bloodstream but doesn’t rid the body of it, says Martin Fussenegger, a bioengineer at ETH Zurich. The new implant instead removes glucose from the body without added drugs, genes or living cells.

The 3-centimeter-long device contains a catalyst made of gold flakes and platinum particles on spongelike graphite. When electricity powers it, the catalyst converts glucose into gluconate, a compound that is easier for the kidneys to flush out in urine. With less glucose available for energy, the body may turn to its fat stores instead, Fussenegger and colleagues suspect. In mice, that shift showed up as higher blood levels of chemicals released when fat breaks down, such as ketones. “This system kind of targets the root cause, which is the energy surplus by glucose in the body,” Fussenegger says.

The implant works like an automatic sugar-removal system: A wearable glucose monitor detects high blood sugar levels and sends readings through a smartphone that switches the implant on. When levels return to a safer range, it switches off. The automated system ran for two weeks in eight mice. The catalyst itself remained able to convert glucose after up to three months under their skin, though the study didn’t establish how long the entire device would last.

And it’s still unknown how well the device would work in people. “This is a potentially promising method,” says David Klonoff, an endocrinologist at Sutter Mills-Peninsula Medical Center in Burlingame, Calif., who was not involved in the study. “But the risks are significant and must be carefully ruled out before it can be safely tested on humans.”

Researchers need to determine how much gluconate the kidneys can clear, Klonoff says. If it builds up, it could disrupt the body’s acid-base balance, causing symptoms such as nausea or confusion; excreting it could also deplete electrolytes such as sodium and potassium, he notes.

Scaling up the device is another challenge. Humans consume about 250 grams of carbohydrates daily, compared with two grams for mice, Klonoff estimates. Meeting that demand could require a much larger implant or multiple devices, he says. In a lab test, a larger device cleared nearly all glucose from about 5 liters of solution, roughly an adult’s blood volume, though not a full day’s glucose intake.

Fussenegger’s team plans to test the device in pigs and sheep before considering human trials. If proven safe and effective, it could offer an alternative to existing diabetes treatments and a new weight-loss option for people regardless of whether they have diabetes, he says.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

#6423. Scientists reach record-low temperature aboard China’s space station

Physicists on China's Tiangong station cooled 20,000 atoms to the coldest temperature in space: 9.7 trillionths of a degree above zero.

For 30 years, physicists have pushed clouds of atoms toward ever lower temperatures, with Earth’s gravity limiting how far they could go.

Now, a speck of gas aboard China’s Tiangong space station has reached what its creators report is a record-low temperature.

There, physicists chilled about 20,000 rubidium atoms to an equivalent temperature of 9.7 trillionths of a degree above absolute zero, which is minus 459.67°F (minus 273.15°C).

The previous record for a cloud like this was 38 trillionths, set in a drop tower on Earth.

The temperature here is a measure of how fast the cloud spreads once released, not a reading from a thermometer. The authors wrote that the result is the lowest they know of.

Xiaoji Zhou and Xuzong Chen of Peking University led the work with Weibiao Chen of the Shanghai Institute of Optics and Fine Mechanics and colleagues at Fudan University.

Their apparatus has been running on the station since October 2022. When they released the atoms, they could still see the cloud seven seconds later.

The usual way to make atoms this cold is to hold them in a trap and let the hottest ones escape, the way steam leaving a cup cools the coffee.

The looser the trap, the colder the atoms that remain. On Earth, though, a trap that is too loose simply drops its atoms. Gravity sets a floor.

That is why laboratories on the ground have stalled around 350 trillionths of a degree in three dimensions.

Drop towers and sounding rockets buy a few seconds of free fall.

NASA’s Cold Atom Laboratory on the International Space Station, which holds atoms with magnetic fields, has reached 52 trillionths and watched clouds for about a second.

The Chinese team used light instead of magnets. Two crossed laser beams make a trap that can hold atoms whatever their magnetic state, which opens up experiments a magnetic trap can’t run.

No one had made a quantum gas this way in orbit before.

The experiment lives in the Cold Atom Physics Rack aboard the space station‘s Mengtian module.

About two million rubidium atoms were loaded into the first trap and the laser power was eased down over about 20 seconds.

As the trap weakened, the gas formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a state in which many atoms share a single quantum state and behave collectively.

Weightlessness turned out to have a cost. On Earth, gravity tilts the trap and helps the hottest atoms spill out.

Without that tilt, evaporation in orbit was slower and less complete, and only about 65% of the atoms joined the condensate, against 89% in an identical setup on the ground.

The team’s fix was a stand-in for gravity. A magnetic field gradient pulled on the atoms whose spins made them magnetic, speeding their escape and pushing the rest into a single, magnetically neutral state.

The fraction in the condensate climbed to 89%, about 23,000 atoms.

Even a condensate isn’t finished cooling. The atoms still push on one another, and when the trap opens that pressure becomes motion.

So the team handed the atoms to a second, wider pair of beams, let the trap relax for just over a second, and then switched it off.

Released, the cloud drifted outward at about 70 to 88 micrometers a second, a few thousandths of an inch per second.

Translated into temperature, that is 9.7 trillionths of a degree, with an uncertainty of roughly three trillionths either way. The atoms were, for practical purposes, barely moving.

The team’s computer simulation of the same steps predicted 7.4 trillionths of a degree, and the authors attributed the difference to jitter in the laser beams.

A cloud that expands this slowly could improve atom interferometers, whose sensitivity can increase with the square of the atoms’ time in free flight.

Seven seconds of free fall in orbit is a very long time by that standard.

The temperature estimate rests on the first two seconds of expansion. Although the cloud remained visible afterward, the later images were too faint to use in the calculation.

The condensate is also small. The authors wrote that a trap whose volume can be tuned should let them hold more atoms.

Their stated goals are to study exotic quantum phases that only appear at these temperatures, and to build an atom interferometer in orbit.

That is a device that could test whether all objects really fall at the same rate.

Both goals would benefit from more atoms and longer free flight. The experiment marks a step toward creating those conditions in orbit.

The full study was published in the journal Science.
